# The Origin of the Horizon Line

Long ago, when the world was newly formed, the Sky and the Sea were madly in love. They embraced so completely that no one could tell where one ended and the other began. The Sky would dive deep into the Sea's waves, and the Sea would leap up into the Sky's clouds.

But their love was chaotic. Storms raged endlessly. Sailors couldn't navigate. Birds couldn't fly. The creatures of the world pleaded with the two lovers to separate, just enough to let life flourish between them.

The Sky and Sea refused, unwilling to part even slightly.

Finally, the Sun intervened. "If you truly love each other," the Sun said, "you will make space for the world you've created together."

Reluctantly, the Sky and Sea agreed to separate. But their love remained so strong that they couldn't bear to part completely. So they created the horizon line—a place where they could meet every dawn and dusk, kissing gently where the eye can see them touch.

Even now, when you look at the horizon, you witness their eternal compromise: apart enough to let the world breathe, yet forever reaching toward each other across the endless distance.

A curious shepherd boy discovered one such stone and brought it to his village. When placed near another singing stone, their hums harmonized into a beautiful melody. The villagers scattered across the mountains, gathering more stones, and soon discovered that each combination created different songs—some joyful, some melancholic, some wild as storms.

Orath heard the music drifting up from the valleys below and descended from his peak. Though the villagers feared him at first, they offered him the stones. As Orath held them, the stones sang their loudest, and he finally understood: his loneliness had created something that brought others together.

From that day forward, Orath lived among the humans, and the singing stones reminded all who heard them that even sorrow can create beauty.
